sentences.text: This dinosaur is easily recognized by a pair of high, thin, arched crests that ran along the top of its skull.
Its mouth contained long, curved, thin, and sideways-compressed teeth, where the lower jaw teeth were much smaller than those in the upper jaw.
The skeleton included 10 neck vertebrae, 14 back vertebrae, and 45 tail vertebrae that contained air sacs.
It was one of the first large predatory dinosaurs, reaching a length of about 7 meters and a weight of approximately 400 kilograms.
Although it was a medium-sized theropod, it was small compared to later predatory dinosaurs.
The species may have grown rapidly, gaining 30 to 35 kilograms per year during its early life stages.
The holotype specimen showed signs of developmental anomalies and healed injuries.
In 2017, this animal was designated the state dinosaur of Connecticut.
Three skeletons were found in northern Arizona in 1940, with the two best-preserved ones collected in 1942.
During the summer of 1942, paleontologist Charles L. Camp led a UCMP field party to search for fossils in Navajo County.
The genus name, meaning "two-crested lizard," was coined by Welles in 1970.
It was likely an active, bipedal predator that may have hunted large animals but also fed on smaller animals and fish.
Early researcher Welles concluded that the animal lacked a powerful bite because of a weak area in the snout called the subnarial gap.
Welles hypothesized that the creature used front teeth for plucking and tearing while using rear teeth for piercing and slicing.
It possessed powerful, flexible forelimbs that were not used for walking.
The hands could grasp, slash, meet each other, and reach two-thirds of the way up the neck.
The holotype specimen showed a groove on a neck vertebra possibly caused by injury and pits on the right arm bone that could be abscesses or artifacts.
Welles concluded the specimens were buried near their death sites with little transport, though the holotype shows signs of scavenger disturbance such as rotated vertebrae and a crushed skull.
Some researchers interpret a resting trace of a Dilophosaurus-like theropod as showing impressions of down-like feathers around the belly and feet.
In 1970, paleontologist Welles revised his earlier 1954 classification of the animal as a megalosaur after discovering it possessed crests.
By 1974, Welles and Robert A. Long classified Dilophosaurus as a ceratosauroid.
Marsh and Rowe concluded in 2020 that all known Dilophosaurus specimens belong to a single taxon, with differences explained by maturity and preservation.
It is debated whether Dilophosaurus belongs to the family Dilophosauridae with Dracovenator, as some researchers do not support this grouping.
Welles named the ichnospecies Dilophosauripus williamsi based on tridactyl footprints that could have been made by Dilophosaurus.

In 1996, Morales and Bulkey estimated that a trackmaker of the ichnogenus Eubrontes would have been 2.83 to 2.99 m tall at the hips, making it unlikely to be Dilophosaurus, which stands 1.50 to 1.75 m tall.

Gierliński and Sabath argued in 2005 that traces resembling modern bird semiplumes found on a track were real feather impressions, not sedimentological artifacts, based on experiments showing algae mats leave similar marks.
Its parent group is Neotheropoda.
Dilophosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically from the Sinemurian to Toarcian stages.
It lived during the Early Jurassic, approximately 196 to 186 million years ago.
The animal is known from the Kayenta Formation and lived alongside dinosaurs like Scutellosaurus and Sarahsaurus.
